name: Jamal Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union, party or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a workers' co-operative, a building firm owned by the people who work in it, about forty of us. We do retrofits on old public housing, mostly blocks from the 1960s: new insulation, new windows, timber-frame extensions on the ground floor flats. Today I was fitting insulated panels on the back of a four-storey block on Orchard Road while the tenants were having breakfast inside. I like that the people we're working for are the people living there, not some fund in another country.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does technology fit into your day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: More than people expect. I use an AI assistant every morning to turn the architect's drawings into cutting lists, and I check the building rules with it when I'm not sure. It translates for two of our crew, Yusuf and Petra, who are still learning the language. My back is fifty-eight years old and has carried a lot of plasterboard, so if there's a machine that lifts, I'm the first to say yes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, shame, I was looking forward to the robot that carries the plasterboard. At the co-op meeting I'd say we keep using the tools that work and stop paying for the ones that don't. Online I'd probably post something a bit sarcastic about all the hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine, honestly, life carries on. I've got the co-op shares, my partner Inès's teaching pension, our flat's paid for. I'd just be slightly disappointed that my back doesn't get any help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I do, keep using the assistant for the cutting lists and the quotes. I'd probably show a few of the older guys how to use it for the dull paperwork, because even a small saving is worth having. I'd plan to retire at sixty-three or so like before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, maybe a bit flat. Like the circus came to town and it was only one clown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day already. What does it actually save you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe forty minutes a day, mostly the cutting lists and the emails to suppliers. That's not nothing, over a year it's a couple of weeks. But it doesn't change who I am or what the job is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the co-op would be most pleased if it fizzled?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Barbara, who runs the accounts, she can't stand all this. She'd be at the next meeting with a big smile. Fair enough, she's been right about plenty of things.

S0.say: I'd say it's a shame, because I wanted the robot that carries plasterboard. At the co-op I'd say keep the tools that work and drop the rest.
S0.think: It's fine for me and life carries on, with the co-op shares, Inès's pension and the flat paid for. I'm just a bit disappointed my back gets no help.
S0.do: Keeps using the AI assistant for cutting lists and quotes and shows older colleagues how to use it for paperwork. Keeps his plan to retire around sixty-three.
S0.feel: Calm and a little flat, like a circus with only one clown.
S0.quote: Like the circus came to town and it was only one clown.
S0.fieldNote: Jamal is the rare older tradesman who is mildly let down by AI fizzling. His enthusiasm is practical and tied to his worn-out back. He is secure and frames everything through the co-op he partly owns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Next scenario. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why workers should own the business. If our co-op buys the machines, the time they save comes back to us as shorter weeks or better pay, not to some shareholder. I'd say that at the co-op meeting, and I'd say it online too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's mostly good news. I'd be the one who already knows how to use the stuff, so I'd be useful right to the end. The risk is for people like Yusuf who are just starting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put a proposal to the co-op in the first month to trial a lifting robot and a layout machine on one job, and I'd volunteer to run the trial. I'd use part of my own shares to back the purchase. And I'd ask to train the apprentices on the new kit, because I'd rather they learn it from us than from a salesman.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, really. A little worried for the young ones, but mostly I'd feel like it's my moment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a layout machine do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a little robot that drives round the floor and draws the lines of every wall from the drawings, so you know where to build. It takes us half a day with a tape and chalk line. I've seen videos, I've not used one yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's mostly good news for you. Is there anything you'd lose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The chalk line, maybe, the bit where two of us measure and argue and get it right. That's where you get to know a new worker. I'd miss that, I'm not going to lie.

S1.say: I'd say this is why workers should own the business. If our co-op buys the machines, the time saved comes back to us, not some shareholder.
S1.think: It's mostly good news, because I'd already know the tools and be useful to the end. The risk is for people like Yusuf who are just starting.
S1.do: Proposes a co-op trial of a lifting robot and a layout machine in the first month and volunteers to run it. Puts part of his own shares behind the purchase and asks to train the apprentices on the kit.
S1.feel: Excited, with a little worry for the young workers. He feels it's his moment.
S1.quote: I'd rather they learn it from us than from a salesman.
S1.fieldNote: Jamal sees steady change as a chance, and his politics shape it: machines are fine if workers own them. He'd put his own money in. His one real loss is the social side of measuring up with a new colleague.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one is much faster. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to decide who owns the robots, us or a handful of billionaires. I'd be loud about it, online, at the co-op, at whatever protests there are. A robot that does everything is either the best thing that happened to working people or the worst, and that's a political choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, honestly, I'd be okay, I'm near the end and I've got savings. But two years is too fast for most people, and I'd look at Yusuf and Petra and my daughter, who's a translator, and I'd worry. Her job would be one of the first gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first few months I'd push the co-op to buy robots before the big firms corner the market, so we'd own them ourselves. I'd join the campaign for a public share in AI companies and vote that way. Once it arrives, I'd step back from site work and help retrain our members, and I'd stop at sixty if the co-op could pay its people without me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not for me but for everyone else. And a bit of a buzz, which I feel guilty about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your daughter's a translator. What would you say to her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm sorry, first. I helped her pay for her degree in languages. Then I'd say we'll help, there's room in our flat and money in the bank, and maybe the co-op needs someone to deal with all the new rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You feel a buzz and feel guilty. Can you say more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've always loved new tools, since my first nail gun. And this is the biggest new tool there's ever been. But I know a man getting excited while his daughter loses her job isn't a pretty picture.

S2.say: I'd say this is the moment to decide who owns the robots, us or a few billionaires. It's either the best or the worst thing for working people, and that's a political choice.
S2.think: I'd be okay, being near the end with savings. But two years is too fast, and I'd worry about Yusuf, Petra and my daughter the translator.
S2.do: Pushes the co-op to buy robots early so its members own them and joins the campaign for a public share in AI companies. Once it arrives, steps back from site work to help retrain members and may stop at sixty.
S2.feel: Uneasy for others, with a buzz of excitement he feels guilty about.
S2.quote: I know a man getting excited while his daughter loses her job isn't a pretty picture.
S2.fieldNote: Jamal is personally secure and drawn to the technology, so his unease is about speed and about his daughter's career. He was frank about the guilt of feeling excited. His response combines ownership, politics and helping others retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's slow it down a little. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ahead of it if we start now. Co-ops, unions and councils should be buying in, training up and deciding the rules together. I'd post that and I'd say it at every meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is the one I like best, to be honest. It's fast enough to matter while I'm still working, but there's time for my daughter and the young ones to move. I'd be in the thick of it for my last few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put about a third of our savings into the co-op's machine fund over two years, which I've talked over with Inès. I'd do a short course in running site robots, the kind the equipment suppliers offer, and I'd become the co-op's person for it. I'd help my daughter look at what she could switch to while her work still pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and actually quite hopeful. Busy, but the good kind of busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A third of your savings is a lot. What did Inès say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She said, as long as it's not the flat. And she's right, the flat is ours and it stays ours. The rest is money that should be working for people, not sitting in a bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two years doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to do it properly. In two years we'd be panic-buying robots to beat the big firms. In five we can choose good ones, train our people and keep everyone on.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to get ahead of it if we start now. Co-ops, unions and councils should buy in, train up and set the rules together.
S3.think: This is the one I like best, fast enough to matter while I'm working but slow enough for young people to move. I'd be in the thick of it.
S3.do: Puts about a third of the family savings into the co-op's machine fund over two years, keeping the flat safe. Takes a supplier course in running site robots and helps his daughter plan a switch.
S3.feel: Calm and quite hopeful, the good kind of busy.
S3.quote: In two years we'd be panic-buying robots to beat the big firms.
S3.fieldNote: Five years is Jamal's ideal: enough speed to be exciting and enough time to bring people along. His investment plan is bold but protects the home. He thinks in terms of choosing the right machines rather than whether to use them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the slowest version. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse for anyone to be left behind. Every young worker should get free training on the new machines. And I'd be saying it as a retired man, so maybe they'd listen less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's gentle. I'd retire at sixty-three before most of it arrives, and I'd watch from the sidelines. I might be a bit jealous, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep pushing the co-op to trial new kit as it comes. After I stop, I'd like to teach evening classes on using AI on site at the trade college, a few hours a week for a bit of money. I'd keep our savings where they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of envy for the young ones who get all the new toys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Jealous of what, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Of the apprentices in 2036 who'll never carry a sheet of plasterboard up three flights. My back would have loved that. I'd be sitting there with my bad back telling them how lucky they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the slow version that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people get lazy because it feels far away. Ten years is long enough for politicians to promise and forget. That's the trap, and I'd say so.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty, so nobody should be left behind and every young worker should get free training on the new machines.
S4.think: For me it's gentle, I'd retire at sixty-three before most of it arrives and watch from the sidelines. I might be a bit jealous.
S4.do: Keeps working and pushing the co-op to trial new equipment. After retiring, plans to teach paid evening classes on using AI on site at the trade college.
S4.feel: Calm, with some envy for the apprentices who get the new machines.
S4.quote: I'd be sitting there with my bad back telling them how lucky they are.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Jamal is comfortable and a little wistful. His one worry is political drift, promises made and forgotten over a long timeline. His retirement plan keeps him close to the technology he enjoys.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it's too fast for people, even if the technology is exciting. What would help is ownership: co-ops, councils and the public owning a share of the machines, so the gains come back to the people who did the work. And free training for everyone, starting now.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask who people trust to run this. I trust the co-op because I can stand up at the meeting and vote. I don't trust a company where I'll never meet anyone who decides anything.

headlineQuote: I don't trust a company where I'll never meet anyone who decides anything.
portrait: Jamal Moreau is a 58-year-old carpenter at a workers' co-operative that retrofits 1960s public housing, a daily AI user whose worn back makes him welcome lifting robots. He is financially secure, with co-op shares, a paid-off flat and a teacher partner. He's calm in nearly every scenario and excited by steady change, which he sees as a chance for workers to own the machines. Only the two-year AGI case makes him uneasy, mainly for his translator daughter and new colleagues, and he admits feeling guilty about his excitement. His answer to every scenario is worker and public ownership of the technology.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because it would come too fast for people even though the technology excites him.
whatWouldHelp: Co-ops, councils and the public owning a share of the machines so the gains go back to workers, plus free training for everyone starting now.
